en: Regarding the *ḍamaruka* [drum-shaped figure]: on a square field whose dimensions are equal to the mouth and divided into twelve parts, one should lay down two Brahma-threads. Holding a thread at the center (Brahman), it is rotated around the navel as far as the opposite corner. By erasing the lines from the outer Brahma-corners, the *ḍamaruka* is formed.

Regarding the *ḍamaru*: on a square surface the size of a mouth, there are twelve parts; having struck two Brahma-lines, one draws from the Brahma-line toward the right and left corners as far as the navel, and by erasing the ends of the Brahma and corner lines, it becomes a *ḍamaru*.

Situated for grasping with the fist and extending to the edge of the small ear, the staff is of mouth-measure; and because of the drawing of a portion of the three-pronged vajra as before within a square field, a trident appears above.

The thickness, which is suitable for grasping by the hand due to its transformation, and the length, reaching to the end of the ears, constitute the handle; on the ground established by the measurement of the face, as before, a three-pointed vajra is extended upward at each of the respective locations, thereby forming three points.

Then, there is the *khaṭvāṅga*, which, like the *samayavajra*, has its head adorned with a *vajra*; below that, it is beautified by three dried skulls; its middle is marked with a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*); and its root is the base of a single-pronged thunderbolt (*kuliśa*). This constitutes one [item].

Then, [the syllable] *kha* is adorned at its tip with the vajra that is like the vajra of the samaya (*samayavajra*). Below that, it is beautified by three withered human corpses and adorned in the center with a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*). Some maintain that a single one-pointed vajra is located at the base.

Above the staff are two dry-faced skulls; upon those heads is a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*); at its navel is a face adorned with a vase, leaves, and other ornaments; above the face is the pledge-vajra (*samayakuliśa*) with five hanging streamers—this is the second [mandala].

On top of the staff are two human heads, one dry and one fresh; upon their crown is a crossed vajra (viśvavajra), in the center of which is a round vase adorned with petals and so forth, from the top of which a samaya-vajra hangs down. This is the second [part].
The staff for both should be thick at the top and slender at the bottom; it should be adorned with small bells and so forth, including a skull, as is aesthetically pleasing.
Both [the upper and lower parts] are thick at the top and slender in the middle, adorned with small bells and the like. As for the head and other parts, they should be made as beautiful as possible.
In a square field measuring one palm-span and divided into twelve parts, the central portion consists of four parts; likewise, the part measured by four parts has the shape of a trident.
The height is four squares, consisting of twelve parts; four parts in the center are for holding the liquor. Likewise, four parts are curved, having the shape of a tip.
When the compass is bent from the eighth-part corner up to the ninth-part corner, the mark of a half-vajra appears above the handle.
The curved blade, extending from the corner of the eighth part to the corner of the ninth part, is the curved knife (kartṛkā); it is adorned with a half-vajra on top of its handle.
As for the skull-cup (*kapāla*):
the skull-cup.
One should know that it is joined with a golden gate and possesses a human head; furthermore,
each skeleton of a Brahmin and the other [castes] is increased by one ear.
The skull of each [caste], beginning with the Brahmin, increases [in size] according to their respective [status].
The skull of one of inferior caste (*hīnavarṇaka*) shall have a hole above the ear;
that of eunuchs has a hole in the back; and that of women is always free of any blemishes.

A head that has become discolored, one with a hole above the ear, or one with a hole in the back or that is split— these are always to be known by the wise and the learned, as well as by mantra-practitioners, as belonging to women.
A line like a string of pearls should be drawn on the forehead and at the temples;
likewise, the wise man, possessing consciousness, should draw what is called the "head" [mark] with a mantra-practitioner.
A mark resembling a string of pearls should be formed on the forehead and the conch-like ears.
The moon [mandala] may consist of one, two, three, or four segments, or have sixteen or twelve spokes;
it should be cow-faced, white and red, and slightly elongated is auspicious. It should be slightly elongated.

In fragments of one, two, three, and four, and in sixteen, twelve, and one [digit], they become the rabbit-marked moon, the elephant-faced [Ganesha], and white and red; somewhat elongated and beautiful,
likewise like a lotus, having the form of a lotus, and yellow, red, and white.
One should accept praiseworthy skull-bowls, but one should avoid those that remain [defective].

Likewise: "Skulls that are praised are those shaped like a lotus or similar to a lotus; yellow, red, or white—such as these are the skulls that should be shown, while all others should be avoided. Thus it is said.
A noose that is well-stretched, coiled, two finger-breadths thick, and marked with a vajra at both ends.
The noose consists of a coil made according to one's own preference, two finger-widths in thickness, and adorned with vajras at both ends.
A four-faced Brahma’s skull from which blood is trickling.
The four-faced one with blood dripping from the throat is the head of Brahmā.
The axe-head is equal in size to the face; it has a handle two cubits long, six finger-breadths in circumference, and is marked with a thunderbolt at the top.
The blade of the *dgra sta* (battle-axe) is the size of the face, while the handle is six finger-widths (*sor*) in circumference and adorned with a vajra at the top.
Likewise, the *aṅkuśa* (hook) is measured at one *vitasti*.
The hook similar to that has a crooked tip one span in height.
Wearing an elephant hide reaching as far as his ears.
The elephant hide is held [stretched] as far as the ears.
The mallet is like a double-vajra, but it possesses a circular handle with a single-pronged point at one end.
The pestle is like a *vicitra* [lotus]; its lower part also has a single-pointed tip, with a rounded handle.

Of a bow measuring ten *tāla*s and four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width, by means of a hollowed-out notch (*sukā*) sixteen finger-breadths long; of a thunderbolt (*vajra*) that is eight finger-breadths in length at its center and nine finger-breadths in circumference, being circular and endowed with the characteristics of a bud, a pericarp, a conch, and so forth.

The bow is ten finger-widths (*aṅgula*) in height and four finger-widths in width; its grip is sixteen finger-widths long, its curved middle is eight finger-widths, and its rounded ends are nine finger-widths; it possesses the characteristics of being fully expanded at the tip and having a well-strung string.
Having firmly positioned the shoulder and back, and grasping [the bow] from the middle with the fist of the extended left arm,

one should look toward the path of the arrow from the right eye for the sake of subjugation (*vaśya*). With the *vajramuṣṭi* [grip], while drawing the arrow drawn back as far as the ear with a roar like a two-armed archer, one should hold it crosswise, slightly rotating the bowl of the hand.

By means of looking with the right eye exactly as an arrow [is aimed], one draws back the vajra-fist bow measuring two cubits up to the tip of the arrow, from the vicinity of the nose and mouth to the ear; then, by moving it slightly, one fully grasps it.

One should have a sword made thirty-six finger-breadths in length, with a blade four finger-breadths wide and situated in the middle of a hilt four finger-breadths long. Its two sides, extending four finger-breadths each, are adorned with the shape of a serpent’s hood. Its center is flattened, measuring one finger-breadth in width, and it is provided with an inner handle-staff (*daṇḍikā*) four finger-breadths in length that serves as an ornament. According to the requirements of the ritual, it should be eight finger-breadths in measure and equipped with a pommel (*pālikā*) shaped like a finger, a leaf, a square, or a half-moon. It should be made so that it shines with a guard (*gañjā*) of two finger-breadths.

A wooden rod thirty-six finger-widths long and four finger-widths wide, held at its center by a ring four finger-widths in diameter; it is beautifully adorned with the form of a nāga’s hood, with four finger-widths branching out from each side, and in its center, it expands like a knob for one finger-width, possessing a beautiful handle four finger-widths long at the end of the base.

In accordance with its function, the sword is eight finger-breadths in length, possesses petals one finger-breadth wide, is square in shape, is provided with gate-keepers in the form of parasols and crescent moons, and is beautifully adorned with a hilt two finger-breadths thick.

The circumference of the nave is one part; outside that, the circumference of the inner rim (garbhanemi) is half a part; further outside, the circumference of the spokes (ārā) is one and a quarter parts; and on the exterior of that, the circumference of the outer rim (nemi) is half a part. This is the measurement for all wheels having four spokes and so forth.

Regarding the wheel: one part [of the total] is for the circular hub; outside of that, half a part is for the circular inner rim (*nemi*); again, outside of that, one part plus a quarter is for the circle of the spokes;
and outside of that, another half a part is for the circular outer rim. This is the measurement for all wheels, such as those with four spokes and so forth.
A small iron ball bound at its tip with chains, a bronze bilva-shaped object,
an arrow-feathered shaft, a javelin, and a sling for the face.
The iron bilva fruit, bound at its tip with iron chains, is the *kaṇaya*. That which is like an arrow, possessing three feathers and the size of a face, is the *kunta*.
Similarly, the *tomara* is long, winged, and shaped like a sword;
the dimensions of the *kunta*, *sellā*, and so forth are not described here as they are well known.

That which is similar to those [weapons], but with a long shaft and a tip shaped like a *tvāṅga* (a type of bird), is the *mahāśara*. As for the dimensions of the *śakti*, *vajra*, and so forth, they have not been described here because they are already well known.
Holding all weapons above the ear is forbidden;
this is the rule for the characteristics of weapons.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the characteristics of the weapons.
